#+TITLE: Compute Performance of the GPU Cost Path — Sync-Point Inventory, Streamed Pipeline, Instrumentation, Ordered Cuts
#+DATE: 2026-08-12
#+PANOPTES_ANGLE: compute-perf

* Summary

The synthesis item-8 claim (cost path is sync-bound, not kernel-bound) is *directionally confirmed by source structure but not yet measured*: every eval runs on the default stream with zero streams/events anywhere in src/, and 5 synchronous `cudaMemcpy` D2H calls per monoplane eval (`render_engine.cu:781-790` ×2, `fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:289-290` ×1, `distance_map_metric.cu:110-119` ×2) each drain the entire device pipeline, leaving the GPU idle across 3 distinct host-block windows per eval. The existing ms/call meter (`optimizer_manager.cpp:1272-1278`) uses `clock()`, which measures CPU process time and *excludes both GPU time and sync-wait time* — so it systematically under-reads a sync-bound pipeline and cannot arbitrate the claim. The removal order that follows is: (0) instrument with nvtx3 + cudaEvent and measure; (1) async-ify the 3 terminal score copies with a single per-eval event wait (pinned buffers already exist — pure win); (2) batch the DIRECT iteration's independent evals with double-buffered eval state so one eval's tail overlaps the next's head; (3) only if the fragment-fill sync remains dominant, remove it via a device-side clamp + fixed grid (the one kernel-level change); (4) fix the meter to wall-clock/event time. Every cut is gated on the oracle (IoU ≥ 0.85) and, where possible, bit-identical cost values.

* Key Findings

** Sync-point inventory (monoplane eval = 14-15 kernel launches + 5 sync D2H)

Per-eval hot path is `CostFunctionManager::costFunctionDIRECT_DILATION` (src/compute/DIRECT_DILATION.cpp:67-106): RenderPrimaryCamera → FastImplantDilationMetric → DistanceMapMetric. Kernel/D2H count verified in source:

- Render (`RenderEngine::Render`, src/compute/render_engine.cu:711-840): `cudaMemset` (:716), ResetKernel (:722), WorldToPixelKernel (:725), BoundingBoxForTrianglesKernel (:746), BoundingBoxSizesKernel (:756), `cub::DeviceScan::ExclusiveSum` (:764), PrepareLaunchPacketKernel (:775), StridePrefixKernel (:812), FillTriangleKernel (:823) — 8 launches + cub internals.
- FastImplantDilationMetric (src/compute/fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:169-295): ResetPixelScoreKernel (:170), EdgeKernel (:218), DilateKernel (:242), DifferenceKernel (:273) — 4 launches.
- DistanceMapMetric (src/compute/distance_map_metric.cu:71-127): 2× Reset (:72,:73) + main kernel (:99) — 3 launches.
- Total ≈ 15 launches (matches the "~15 kernel launches" figure) + 5 synchronous D2H `cudaMemcpy`.
- Biplane adds a full second Render + FastImplantDilationMetric (+11 launches, +3 D2H).
- Confidence: high
- Relevance: this is the count synthesis item 8 was built on; the per-sync *cost* is the part that needs measurement (Cut 0).

The 5 syncs, classified by removability:

| # | file:line | payload | consumer | class |
|---|-----------|---------|----------|-------|
| 1 | render_engine.cu:781-785 | bounding box, 4×int, pinned (`gpu_image.cu:21-22`) | host crop computation for metric launch grids (fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:201-207, distance_map_metric.cu:83-89) | structural mid-eval: host needs bbox to *size* the metric launches; removable only by moving crop to device (kernel change) |
| 2 | render_engine.cu:786-790 | fragment_fill, 1×int, pinned (`render_engine.cu:248-249`) | host overflow check (:795-808) + grid dims of StridePrefix (:812-816) and FillTriangle (:823-827) | structural mid-eval: data-dependent launch; removable via device-side clamp + fixed grid (Cut 3) |
| 3 | fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:289-290 | pixel score, 1×int, pinned (`gpu_metrics.cu:7-11`) | return value of the metric | terminal — async-able now (Cut 1) |
| 4 | distance_map_metric.cu:110-114 | distance_map_score, 1×int, pinned (`gpu_metrics.cu:52-56`) | return value | terminal — async-able now (Cut 1) |
| 5 | distance_map_metric.cu:115-119 | edge_pixels_count, 1×int, pinned (`gpu_metrics.cu:62-65`) | return value | terminal — async-able now (Cut 1) |

Cost nuance: syncs #1 and #2 are back-to-back, so the *fragment* copy (:786-790) waits on the same pipeline drain as the bbox copy and returns almost immediately — the exposed stall is the single drain before them, not two. Similarly #4+#5 share one drain. So the per-eval cost is really ~3 host-block windows (render-head drain, fast-implant drain, distance-map drain), each = GPU idle during host wake + driver launch latency, plus 5× driver round-trip overhead for the sync calls themselves. All targets are already page-locked, so `cudaMemcpyAsync` conversion needs no allocation work.

- Confidence: high
- Relevance: terminal copies (3 of 5) are trivially removable; the 2 render syncs are the structural ones — one of which (fragment_fill) has a clean kernel-level removal, the other (bbox) does not without moving crop math onto the device (which would change launch grids — interaction with 02's metric-math semantics and 04's architecture shape).

** The ms/call meter cannot see GPU time — and under-reads when sync-bound

`optimizer_manager.cpp:1272-1278`:

```cpp
if ((clock() - update_screen_clock_) > 33) {
    emit UpdateDisplay(
        static_cast<double>(clock() - start_clock_) /
            static_cast<double>(opt.GetCostFunctionCalls()),
        ...);
    update_screen_clock_ = clock();
}
```

`clock()` on Linux returns *process CPU time* (user+sys), not wall time. A thread blocked in a synchronous `cudaMemcpy` is sleeping in the driver — it accrues no CPU time. So the meter excludes not only GPU kernel time but also the sync-wait time itself: a sync-bound pipeline reads as *artificially low* ms/call. The meter therefore cannot distinguish "fast" from "GPU idle"; it is directionally misleading for exactly the hypothesis at issue. Any before/after comparison must use a wall-clock meter (std::chrono or cudaEvent), not the existing one.

- Confidence: high (semantics of clock() on Linux; meter code verified)
- Relevance: the user's requirement "a before/after ms/call meter that includes GPU time via events" is not optional polish — the existing meter would fail to show the win, and could even show a *worse* number if a cut moves work from GPU-idle time into CPU time.

** Determinism: int atomicAdd/atomicSub reductions are value-deterministic

All cost-path reductions are integer atomics on single counters:
- DifferenceKernel: `atomicAdd(&result[0], 1)` / `atomicSub(&result[0], 1)` (src/compute/fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:145,147)
- DistanceMapMetric_Kernel: `atomicAdd(&edge_pixel_count[0], 1)`, `atomicAdd(&distance_map_score[0], distance_map[orig_loc])` (src/compute/distance_map_metric.cu:46-47)
- WhitePixelSum / IOUKernel: `atomicAdd` (src/compute/gpu_metrics.cu:129, src/compute/iou.cu:66-72)

Integer addition is commutative and associative — the final value is independent of execution order. Given identical launch configs and identical inputs, every run yields bit-identical scores. Launch configs depend only on the bounding box (a pure function of pose + model), so the same pose sequence reproduces the same grids and the same results. The known order-nondeterministic path (DRR float atomicAdd) is NOT in the DIRECT_DILATION cost path. Consequences:
1. Bit-identical results after Cuts 1-2 are achievable and verifiable by diffing a recorded pose→score sequence against baseline.
2. Cut 3 must preserve the per-thread work for threads `< fragment_fill` exactly (only add an early-exit clamp for threads `>=`), and must not change the cub scan — then rendered output stays bit-identical.
- Confidence: high
- Relevance: the user's "bit-identical if possible" bar is real; it also gives the oracle a cheap extra gate (compare per-frame optimized pose + cost value to the baseline run, not just IoU).

** Allocation hoisting verified — nothing allocates in the eval path; buffers are pinned

- GPUMetrics ctor allocates all host score buffers via `cudaHostAlloc` and all device score buffers via `cudaMalloc` once (src/compute/gpu_metrics.cu:7-65); destructor frees (same file:68-95).
- RenderEngine::InitializeCUDA allocates all triangle/bounding-box buffers once (src/compute/render_engine.cu:248-323), including CUB scan storage via the size-query idiom (:311-320) — `cub_storage_bytes_` is fixed after init, so the per-eval `cub::DeviceScan::ExclusiveSum` at :764 is a plain launch with no allocation.
- `fragment_fill_` (render_engine.cu:248-249) and `bounding_box_` (src/compute/gpu_image.cu:21-22) are pinned host memory.
- The eval path (`costFunctionDIRECT_DILATION`) performs no cudaMalloc/cudaHostAlloc/free. The per-eval churn is 5 D2H copies, not allocations.
- Confidence: high
- Relevance: Cut 1 (async copies) requires zero allocation work — the pinned targets exist. The "scratch-buffer metrics" ask is already satisfied in the GPU cost path; the per-frame churn the earlier synthesis flagged (GPUImage::UploadImageToGPU reallocating on upload) is outside the eval path.

** nvtx: dependency present, zero instrumentation, and CMake never consumes -DLIBNVTOOLSEXT

- `pixi.toml:17` declares `nvtx = "*"`; the lock resolves it to the *Python* package nvtx-0.2.10 (pixi.lock:257) plus cuda-nvtx-12.4.99 (pixi.lock:63).
- `pixi.toml:76` passes `-DLIBNVTOOLSEXT=$CONDA_PREFIX/lib/libnvToolsExt.so.1` to the configure task, but grep of CMakeLists.txt and src/compute/CMakeLists.txt finds no consumer of that variable — it is dead config. `jtml_compute` links only `CUDA::cublas CUDA::cudart CUDA::curand` (src/compute/CMakeLists.txt:60-65).
- grep for nvtx/nvToolsExt across src/ and include/: zero hits. The scaffolding exists; no markers exist.
- The good news: the C++ nvtx3 API (`<nvtx3/nvtx3.hpp>`) is header-only and ships with the CUDA toolkit; `CMAKE_CUDA_TOOLKIT_INCLUDE_DIRECTORIES` is already on jtml_compute's include path (src/compute/CMakeLists.txt:70-72, CMakeLists.txt:64,70), so `#include <nvtx3/nvtx3.hpp>` compiles with *no CMake or link changes*. (The C API `nvtxRangePushA` would need libnvToolsExt linked — avoid it.)
- Nsight availability: `nsight-compute` 2024.1 (ncu) is in the environment (pixi.lock:253); `nsight-systems` (nsys) is NOT (no nsys in pixi.lock) — the profiling plan needs `pixi add nsight-systems` or a system nsys.
- Confidence: high
- Relevance: the "nvtx declared but zero-instrumented" claim verified exactly; the instrumentation plan below is a header include + ~10 range annotations, no build-system surgery.

** The DIRECT loop is sequential, but each iteration's evals are mutually independent — batchable without changing results

`DirectOptimizer::Run` (src/domain/direct_optimizer.cpp:27-58) evaluates the unit center once, then loops ConvexHull → TrisectPotentiallyOptimal. In TrisectPotentiallyOptimal (:113-163), for each potentially-optimal hyperbox, two changed-center points are evaluated sequentially:

```cpp
changed_hyperbox_a->value_ = EvaluateCostFunction(changed_hyperbox_a->GetCenter());
data_.AddHyperBox(changed_hyperbox_a);
changed_hyperbox_b->value_ = EvaluateCostFunction(changed_hyperbox_b->GetCenter());
data_.AddHyperBox(changed_hyperbox_b);
```

Both centers derive from the pre-loop snapshot (`potentially_optimal_hyperboxes_`, :116-118); B's pose does not depend on A's score; the loop does not re-enter ConvexHull until all boxes are processed. So per iteration, all 2×N_optimal evals are pairwise independent and can be enqueued back-to-back with a single terminal wait, replaying the per-eval bookkeeping (best-value update + AddHyperBox + improvement callbacks) in the original order afterward — yielding identical stored values, identical optimum, and identical callback sequences. This is the algorithm-level enabler for pipelining; it does not touch GPU code.

- Confidence: high (code path verified; replay-order preserves observable behavior)
- Relevance: this makes the cheapest big win (Cut 2) available without kernel rewrites — matching the user's "per-eval sync removal, not kernel rewrites" lean.

** In-place metric composition constrains streaming: evals must be double-buffered

FastImplantDilationMetric writes *into* the rendered buffer: EdgeKernel writes EDGE_PIXEL into `rendered_image->GetDeviceImagePointer()` (fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:218-240), DilateKernel writes DILATED_PIXEL into it (:242-271), and DistanceMapMetric then reads that same mutated buffer for `EDGE_PIXEL` (distance_map_metric.cu:46-50). Order within an eval is fixed: Render → edge/dilate (in place) → difference (score 1) → distance-map over the edge pixels (score 2). Consequently:
- The two metrics cannot run concurrently on one buffer, and the next eval's Render (`cudaMemset` at render_engine.cu:716) cannot start until the current eval's last metric kernel finishes reading the image.
- Overlapping eval N's tail with eval N+1's head therefore requires a second GPUImage render output (+ duplicate score buffers), i.e. double-buffered eval state. This is the core of the streamed-pipeline design below and the main structural interaction with 04's architecture shape.
- The biplane path has a free overlap: secondary Render uses a different camera's buffers (gpu_model.cu:144-146), so with async terminal copies the primary metrics' D2H overlaps the secondary render kernels on the same stream with no double-buffering.
- Confidence: high
- Relevance: sets the boundary of what streams can buy; single-stream ordering is mostly sufficient once copies are async — the default stream already serializes correctly, so the minimal design needs no multi-stream complexity.

** Miscellaneous hot-path details

- `Render()` opens with `cudaGetLastError()` per eval, self-annotated "MAYBE DELETE TO SAVE TIME?" (render_engine.cu:713) — a per-eval driver round trip, cheap but pointless in a hot loop where the tail of the function already returns `cudaGetLastError()` (:839). Delete it.
- Per-eval pose upload: none. `SetPose` is host-side (render_engine.cu:354-377); WorldToPixelKernel receives pose scalars as kernel arguments (:725-744). No H2D traffic per eval.
- `WriteImage`/`GetcvMatImage` D2H copies (render_engine.cu:852-856, :880-884) are debug/visualization only — off the hot path.
- The fragment-overflow guard is `fragment_fill_[0] > maximum_stride_size * (threads_per_block - 1)` (render_engine.cu:795-808; constants in include/compute/cuda_launch_parameters.h: maximum_stride_size = 10,000,000, threads_per_block = 256) — i.e. the stride-prefix buffer (10M ints, 40 MB) bounds the algorithm at ~2.55G fragments. This check is the reason sync #2 sits mid-eval.
- Confidence: high
- Relevance: cheap wins to fold into Cut 1 (delete the stray cudaGetLastError) and context for the overflow semantics Cut 3 must preserve.

* The streamed-pipeline design

Goal: keep the GPU busy across evals by removing host-block windows, without multi-stream complexity (default-stream ordering already encodes the dependencies).

- **Phase-separated eval API.** Split the cost callback into *enqueue* (launch all kernels + `cudaMemcpyAsync` terminal copies into the existing pinned buffers + `cudaEventRecord`) and *wait* (read scores after the event). For the non-batched path the wait is immediate; for the batched path it is deferred to the end of the iteration.
- **Double-buffered eval state.** Two GPUImage render outputs (or two device images + one swapped GPUImage) plus a second set of dev score buffers (dev_pixel_score_, dev_distance_map_score_, dev_edge_pixels_count_ — either a second GPUMetrics or buffer arrays). Eval A's metric kernels read image A while eval B's Render memset+writes image B.
- **Iteration batching (DirectOptimizer).** New batch surface on the optimizer (e.g. an optional `batch_cost` callback `std::vector<double>(std::vector<Point6D>)` or a deferred-result API): TrisectPotentiallyOptimal collects the iteration's poses, the cost layer enqueues all evals back-to-back (alternating buffers A/B/A/B...), the mid-eval fragment sync of eval k waits while eval k-1's tail runs on the GPU, and one terminal event wait per iteration harvests all scores; bookkeeping replayed in original order (identical values, identical callback sequence).
- **What stays synchronous.** The fragment-fill D2H (render_engine.cu:786-790) remains mid-eval in Cuts 1-2 — but in the batched design its wait overlaps the *previous* eval's already-enqueued kernels, so it stops being an idle bubble. Only Cut 3 removes it entirely.
- **Biplane overlap for free.** Keep the primary metrics' async copies outstanding while enqueuing the secondary Render + FastImplantDilationMetric (different camera buffers, default-stream order is safe); wait once at the end. No double-buffer needed for this one.
- **Streams vs. single stream.** Two explicit streams (copy stream for the D2H + compute stream for kernels, joined by events) are an optional refinement once events exist; the default-stream version captures most of the win with less risk. 04's architecture angle owns the broader backend shape; the seam here is only "eval state is double-buffered and the cost layer can enqueue before it waits."

* nvtx instrumentation plan

Ranges (nvtx3 header-only, `#include <nvtx3/nvtx3.hpp>`, no link/CMake change; compile in always, they are ~ns overhead):

- **Per-eval** (the range that makes the sync structure visible): wrap `CostFunctionManager::callActiveCostFunction` (src/compute/CostFunctionManager.cpp:276-298) or the cost lambda in `OptimizerManager::RunDirectStage` (optimizer_manager.cpp:1238-1248) — name it "eval", optionally annotate the stage (trunk/branch/leaf) via `nvtx3::scoped_range`.
- **Per-stage within an eval**: `RenderEngine::Render` (render_engine.cu:711), `GPUMetrics::FastImplantDilationMetric` (fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:169), `GPUMetrics::DistanceMapMetric` (distance_map_metric.cu:71).
- **Per-iteration**: the DirectOptimizer `Run` loop body (direct_optimizer.cpp:41-49) — this makes the batch boundary visible once Cut 2 lands.
- **Per-frame**: `OptimizerManager::Optimize` frame-loop body (optimizer_manager.cpp:970-1050 region; the frame loop sets budgets at :991-993) — name it "frame N".
- **Per-sync markers**: `nvtx3::mark` immediately before each of the 5 D2H copies (render_engine.cu:781,786; fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:289; distance_map_metric.cu:110,115) so Nsight shows exactly which sync drains what.

Tooling: `ncu` (nsight-compute 2024.1) is already in the environment for kernel-level data (FillTriangleKernel, DilateKernel, DistanceMapMetric_Kernel); `nsys` (Nsight Systems) must be added (`pixi add nsight-systems`) or used from the system. Capture: `nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --cuda-memory-usage=true .build/bin/jtml_test_oracle` run under a small eval budget, then a production-budget capture of a single frame. Headless default is preserved: instrumentation is inside jtml_compute and inert without a profiler attached.

* Measurement protocol (first profiling run)

1. **Event-based per-eval wall clock** in `test/oracle/oracle_test.cpp`: `cudaEventRecord` start/stop around `p.trunk->callActiveCostFunction()` inside the DirectOptimizer cost lambda (oracle_test.cpp:286-290), accumulating per-eval mean/p50/p95 across the budget. Record the same for `Render()` alone, `FastImplantDilationMetric` alone, `DistanceMapMetric` alone.
2. **Compare against the clock() meter** (optimizer_manager.cpp:1274): capture both simultaneously in a harness run; quantify the gap. Expect event-time > clock()-time whenever syncs or kernels dominate — that gap is the proof of the item-8 claim's magnitude.
3. **Nsight Systems trace** (with the nvtx ranges above): per-eval breakdown = kernel time (sum of ~15 kernel spans) vs. sync stall (gaps between the last kernel before each D2H and the first kernel after the wait) vs. driver/launch overhead. The decisive number: total GPU-active time per eval vs. total wall time per eval.
4. **Nsight Compute** on FillTriangleKernel and DilateKernel: confirm they are memory/latency-bound small kernels (no hidden fat kernel), which justifies treating kernel time as roughly irreducible and sync time as the target.
5. **Bit-identity harness**: a recorded fixed pose sequence (e.g. first 1000 evals of the oracle's frame 0) dumped as (pose → cost) pairs; re-run after each cut and diff — must be identical (int-atomic reductions make this achievable; see determinism finding).
6. **Gate structure for every cut**: (a) headless suite green (`pixi run test`), (b) oracle green (IoU ≥ 0.85 on all 3 frames, oracle_test.cpp:245,333; TIMEOUT 3600 in test/CMakeLists.txt:1253), (c) bit-identity diff empty where claimed, (d) measured per-eval event-time improvement ≥ the cut's predicted Δ (a cut that doesn't move the needle gets reverted — measure-first discipline).

Net effect: 3 sync round trips become 1 event wait; the distance-map pair shares one drain with the fast-implant score; the copies overlap each other and the kernels' tails. Gate: oracle green; per-eval event-time down by measured Δ; bit-identity diff empty. A CPU rasterizer + dilation port is a separate large project with no current consumer; if CPU-side coverage of the cost *math* is wanted, that belongs to 02's metric-math tests (host-side reference implementations), not a render engine port.

#+TITLE: Compute Performance of the GPU Cost Path — Sync-Point Inventory, Streamed Pipeline, Instrumentation, Ordered Cuts
#+DATE: 2026-08-12
#+PANOPTES_ANGLE: compute-perf

* Summary

The synthesis item-8 claim (cost path is sync-bound, not kernel-bound) is *directionally confirmed by source structure but not yet measured*: every eval runs on the default stream with zero streams/events anywhere in src/, and 5 synchronous `cudaMemcpy` D2H calls per monoplane eval (`render_engine.cu:781-790` ×2, `fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:289-290` ×1, `distance_map_metric.cu:110-119` ×2) each drain the entire device pipeline, leaving the GPU idle across 3 distinct host-block windows per eval. The existing ms/call meter (`optimizer_manager.cpp:1272-1278`) uses `clock()`, which measures CPU process time and *excludes both GPU time and sync-wait time* — so it systematically under-reads a sync-bound pipeline and cannot arbitrate the claim. The removal order that follows is: (0) instrument with nvtx3 + cudaEvent and measure; (1) async-ify the 3 terminal score copies with a single per-eval event wait (pinned buffers already exist — pure win); (2) batch the DIRECT iteration's independent evals with double-buffered eval state so one eval's tail overlaps the next's head; (3) only if the fragment-fill sync remains dominant, remove it via a device-side clamp + fixed grid (the one kernel-level change); (4) fix the meter to wall-clock/event time. Every cut is gated on the oracle (IoU ≥ 0.85) and, where possible, bit-identical cost values.

* Key Findings

** Sync-point inventory (monoplane eval = 14-15 kernel launches + 5 sync D2H)

Per-eval hot path is `CostFunctionManager::costFunctionDIRECT_DILATION` (src/compute/DIRECT_DILATION.cpp:67-106): RenderPrimaryCamera → FastImplantDilationMetric → DistanceMapMetric. Kernel/D2H count verified in source:

- Render (`RenderEngine::Render`, src/compute/render_engine.cu:711-840): `cudaMemset` (:716), ResetKernel (:722), WorldToPixelKernel (:725), BoundingBoxForTrianglesKernel (:746), BoundingBoxSizesKernel (:756), `cub::DeviceScan::ExclusiveSum` (:764), PrepareLaunchPacketKernel (:775), StridePrefixKernel (:812), FillTriangleKernel (:823) — 8 launches + cub internals.
- FastImplantDilationMetric (src/compute/fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:169-295): ResetPixelScoreKernel (:170), EdgeKernel (:218), DilateKernel (:242), DifferenceKernel (:273) — 4 launches.
- DistanceMapMetric (src/compute/distance_map_metric.cu:71-127): 2× Reset (:72,:73) + main kernel (:99) — 3 launches.
- Total ≈ 15 launches (matches the "~15 kernel launches" figure) + 5 synchronous D2H `cudaMemcpy`.
- Biplane adds a full second Render + FastImplantDilationMetric (+11 launches, +3 D2H).
- Confidence: high
- Relevance: this is the count synthesis item 8 was built on; the per-sync *cost* is the part that needs measurement (Cut 0).

The 5 syncs, classified by removability:

| # | file:line | payload | consumer | class |
|---|-----------|---------|----------|-------|
| 1 | render_engine.cu:781-785 | bounding box, 4×int, pinned (`gpu_image.cu:21-22`) | host crop computation for metric launch grids (fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:201-207, distance_map_metric.cu:83-89) | structural mid-eval: host needs bbox to *size* the metric launches; removable only by moving crop to device (kernel change) |
| 2 | render_engine.cu:786-790 | fragment_fill, 1×int, pinned (`render_engine.cu:248-249`) | host overflow check (:795-808) + grid dims of StridePrefix (:812-816) and FillTriangle (:823-827) | structural mid-eval: data-dependent launch; removable via device-side clamp + fixed grid (Cut 3) |
| 3 | fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:289-290 | pixel score, 1×int, pinned (`gpu_metrics.cu:7-11`) | return value of the metric | terminal — async-able now (Cut 1) |
| 4 | distance_map_metric.cu:110-114 | distance_map_score, 1×int, pinned (`gpu_metrics.cu:52-56`) | return value | terminal — async-able now (Cut 1) |
| 5 | distance_map_metric.cu:115-119 | edge_pixels_count, 1×int, pinned (`gpu_metrics.cu:62-65`) | return value | terminal — async-able now (Cut 1) |

Cost nuance: syncs #1 and #2 are back-to-back, so the *fragment* copy (:786-790) waits on the same pipeline drain as the bbox copy and returns almost immediately — the exposed stall is the single drain before them, not two. Similarly #4+#5 share one drain. So the per-eval cost is really ~3 host-block windows (render-head drain, fast-implant drain, distance-map drain), each = GPU idle during host wake + driver launch latency, plus 5× driver round-trip overhead for the sync calls themselves. All targets are already page-locked, so `cudaMemcpyAsync` conversion needs no allocation work.

- Confidence: high
- Relevance: terminal copies (3 of 5) are trivially removable; the 2 render syncs are the structural ones — one of which (fragment_fill) has a clean kernel-level removal, the other (bbox) does not without moving crop math onto the device (which would change launch grids — interaction with 02's metric-math semantics and 04's architecture shape).

** The ms/call meter cannot see GPU time — and under-reads when sync-bound

`optimizer_manager.cpp:1272-1278`:

```cpp
if ((clock() - update_screen_clock_) > 33) {
    emit UpdateDisplay(
        static_cast<double>(clock() - start_clock_) /
            static_cast<double>(opt.GetCostFunctionCalls()),
        ...);
    update_screen_clock_ = clock();
}
```

`clock()` on Linux returns *process CPU time* (user+sys), not wall time. A thread blocked in a synchronous `cudaMemcpy` is sleeping in the driver — it accrues no CPU time. So the meter excludes not only GPU kernel time but also the sync-wait time itself: a sync-bound pipeline reads as *artificially low* ms/call. The meter therefore cannot distinguish "fast" from "GPU idle"; it is directionally misleading for exactly the hypothesis at issue. Any before/after comparison must use a wall-clock meter (std::chrono or cudaEvent), not the existing one.

- Confidence: high (semantics of clock() on Linux; meter code verified)
- Relevance: the user's requirement "a before/after ms/call meter that includes GPU time via events" is not optional polish — the existing meter would fail to show the win, and could even show a *worse* number if a cut moves work from GPU-idle time into CPU time.

** Determinism: int atomicAdd/atomicSub reductions are value-deterministic

All cost-path reductions are integer atomics on single counters:
- DifferenceKernel: `atomicAdd(&result[0], 1)` / `atomicSub(&result[0], 1)` (src/compute/fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:145,147)
- DistanceMapMetric_Kernel: `atomicAdd(&edge_pixel_count[0], 1)`, `atomicAdd(&distance_map_score[0], distance_map[orig_loc])` (src/compute/distance_map_metric.cu:46-47)
- WhitePixelSum / IOUKernel: `atomicAdd` (src/compute/gpu_metrics.cu:129, src/compute/iou.cu:66-72)

Integer addition is commutative and associative — the final value is independent of execution order. Given identical launch configs and identical inputs, every run yields bit-identical scores. Launch configs depend only on the bounding box (a pure function of pose + model), so the same pose sequence reproduces the same grids and the same results. The known order-nondeterministic path (DRR float atomicAdd) is NOT in the DIRECT_DILATION cost path. Consequences:
1. Bit-identical results after Cuts 1-2 are achievable and verifiable by diffing a recorded pose→score sequence against baseline.
2. Cut 3 must preserve the per-thread work for threads `< fragment_fill` exactly (only add an early-exit clamp for threads `>=`), and must not change the cub scan — then rendered output stays bit-identical.
- Confidence: high
- Relevance: the user's "bit-identical if possible" bar is real; it also gives the oracle a cheap extra gate (compare per-frame optimized pose + cost value to the baseline run, not just IoU).

** Allocation hoisting verified — nothing allocates in the eval path; buffers are pinned

- GPUMetrics ctor allocates all host score buffers via `cudaHostAlloc` and all device score buffers via `cudaMalloc` once (src/compute/gpu_metrics.cu:7-65); destructor frees (same file:68-95).
- RenderEngine::InitializeCUDA allocates all triangle/bounding-box buffers once (src/compute/render_engine.cu:248-323), including CUB scan storage via the size-query idiom (:311-320) — `cub_storage_bytes_` is fixed after init, so the per-eval `cub::DeviceScan::ExclusiveSum` at :764 is a plain launch with no allocation.
- `fragment_fill_` (render_engine.cu:248-249) and `bounding_box_` (src/compute/gpu_image.cu:21-22) are pinned host memory.
- The eval path (`costFunctionDIRECT_DILATION`) performs no cudaMalloc/cudaHostAlloc/free. The per-eval churn is 5 D2H copies, not allocations.
- Confidence: high
- Relevance: Cut 1 (async copies) requires zero allocation work — the pinned targets exist. The "scratch-buffer metrics" ask is already satisfied in the GPU cost path; the per-frame churn the earlier synthesis flagged (GPUImage::UploadImageToGPU reallocating on upload) is outside the eval path.

** nvtx: dependency present, zero instrumentation, and CMake never consumes -DLIBNVTOOLSEXT

- `pixi.toml:17` declares `nvtx = "*"`; the lock resolves it to the *Python* package nvtx-0.2.10 (pixi.lock:257) plus cuda-nvtx-12.4.99 (pixi.lock:63).
- `pixi.toml:76` passes `-DLIBNVTOOLSEXT=$CONDA_PREFIX/lib/libnvToolsExt.so.1` to the configure task, but grep of CMakeLists.txt and src/compute/CMakeLists.txt finds no consumer of that variable — it is dead config. `jtml_compute` links only `CUDA::cublas CUDA::cudart CUDA::curand` (src/compute/CMakeLists.txt:60-65).
- grep for nvtx/nvToolsExt across src/ and include/: zero hits. The scaffolding exists; no markers exist.
- The good news: the C++ nvtx3 API (`<nvtx3/nvtx3.hpp>`) is header-only and ships with the CUDA toolkit; `CMAKE_CUDA_TOOLKIT_INCLUDE_DIRECTORIES` is already on jtml_compute's include path (src/compute/CMakeLists.txt:70-72, CMakeLists.txt:64,70), so `#include <nvtx3/nvtx3.hpp>` compiles with *no CMake or link changes*. (The C API `nvtxRangePushA` would need libnvToolsExt linked — avoid it.)
- Nsight availability: `nsight-compute` 2024.1 (ncu) is in the environment (pixi.lock:253); `nsight-systems` (nsys) is NOT (no nsys in pixi.lock) — the profiling plan needs `pixi add nsight-systems` or a system nsys.
- Confidence: high
- Relevance: the "nvtx declared but zero-instrumented" claim verified exactly; the instrumentation plan below is a header include + ~10 range annotations, no build-system surgery.

** The DIRECT loop is sequential, but each iteration's evals are mutually independent — batchable without changing results

`DirectOptimizer::Run` (src/domain/direct_optimizer.cpp:27-58) evaluates the unit center once, then loops ConvexHull → TrisectPotentiallyOptimal. In TrisectPotentiallyOptimal (:113-163), for each potentially-optimal hyperbox, two changed-center points are evaluated sequentially:

```cpp
changed_hyperbox_a->value_ = EvaluateCostFunction(changed_hyperbox_a->GetCenter());
data_.AddHyperBox(changed_hyperbox_a);
changed_hyperbox_b->value_ = EvaluateCostFunction(changed_hyperbox_b->GetCenter());
data_.AddHyperBox(changed_hyperbox_b);
```

Both centers derive from the pre-loop snapshot (`potentially_optimal_hyperboxes_`, :116-118); B's pose does not depend on A's score; the loop does not re-enter ConvexHull until all boxes are processed. So per iteration, all 2×N_optimal evals are pairwise independent and can be enqueued back-to-back with a single terminal wait, replaying the per-eval bookkeeping (best-value update + AddHyperBox + improvement callbacks) in the original order afterward — yielding identical stored values, identical optimum, and identical callback sequences. This is the algorithm-level enabler for pipelining; it does not touch GPU code.

- Confidence: high (code path verified; replay-order preserves observable behavior)
- Relevance: this makes the cheapest big win (Cut 2) available without kernel rewrites — matching the user's "per-eval sync removal, not kernel rewrites" lean.

** In-place metric composition constrains streaming: evals must be double-buffered

FastImplantDilationMetric writes *into* the rendered buffer: EdgeKernel writes EDGE_PIXEL into `rendered_image->GetDeviceImagePointer()` (fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:218-240), DilateKernel writes DILATED_PIXEL into it (:242-271), and DistanceMapMetric then reads that same mutated buffer for `EDGE_PIXEL` (distance_map_metric.cu:46-50). Order within an eval is fixed: Render → edge/dilate (in place) → difference (score 1) → distance-map over the edge pixels (score 2). Consequently:
- The two metrics cannot run concurrently on one buffer, and the next eval's Render (`cudaMemset` at render_engine.cu:716) cannot start until the current eval's last metric kernel finishes reading the image.
- Overlapping eval N's tail with eval N+1's head therefore requires a second GPUImage render output (+ duplicate score buffers), i.e. double-buffered eval state. This is the core of the streamed-pipeline design below and the main structural interaction with 04's architecture shape.
- The biplane path has a free overlap: secondary Render uses a different camera's buffers (gpu_model.cu:144-146), so with async terminal copies the primary metrics' D2H overlaps the secondary render kernels on the same stream with no double-buffering.
- Confidence: high
- Relevance: sets the boundary of what streams can buy; single-stream ordering is mostly sufficient once copies are async — the default stream already serializes correctly, so the minimal design needs no multi-stream complexity.

** Miscellaneous hot-path details

- `Render()` opens with `cudaGetLastError()` per eval, self-annotated "MAYBE DELETE TO SAVE TIME?" (render_engine.cu:713) — a per-eval driver round trip, cheap but pointless in a hot loop where the tail of the function already returns `cudaGetLastError()` (:839). Delete it.
- Per-eval pose upload: none. `SetPose` is host-side (render_engine.cu:354-377); WorldToPixelKernel receives pose scalars as kernel arguments (:725-744). No H2D traffic per eval.
- `WriteImage`/`GetcvMatImage` D2H copies (render_engine.cu:852-856, :880-884) are debug/visualization only — off the hot path.
- The fragment-overflow guard is `fragment_fill_[0] > maximum_stride_size * (threads_per_block - 1)` (render_engine.cu:795-808; constants in include/compute/cuda_launch_parameters.h: maximum_stride_size = 10,000,000, threads_per_block = 256) — i.e. the stride-prefix buffer (10M ints, 40 MB) bounds the algorithm at ~2.55G fragments. This check is the reason sync #2 sits mid-eval.
- Confidence: high
- Relevance: cheap wins to fold into Cut 1 (delete the stray cudaGetLastError) and context for the overflow semantics Cut 3 must preserve.

* The streamed-pipeline design

Goal: keep the GPU busy across evals by removing host-block windows, without multi-stream complexity (default-stream ordering already encodes the dependencies).

- **Phase-separated eval API.** Split the cost callback into *enqueue* (launch all kernels + `cudaMemcpyAsync` terminal copies into the existing pinned buffers + `cudaEventRecord`) and *wait* (read scores after the event). For the non-batched path the wait is immediate; for the batched path it is deferred to the end of the iteration.
- **Double-buffered eval state.** Two GPUImage render outputs (or two device images + one swapped GPUImage) plus a second set of dev score buffers (dev_pixel_score_, dev_distance_map_score_, dev_edge_pixels_count_ — either a second GPUMetrics or buffer arrays). Eval A's metric kernels read image A while eval B's Render memset+writes image B.
- **Iteration batching (DirectOptimizer).** New batch surface on the optimizer (e.g. an optional `batch_cost` callback `std::vector<double>(std::vector<Point6D>)` or a deferred-result API): TrisectPotentiallyOptimal collects the iteration's poses, the cost layer enqueues all evals back-to-back (alternating buffers A/B/A/B...), the mid-eval fragment sync of eval k waits while eval k-1's tail runs on the GPU, and one terminal event wait per iteration harvests all scores; bookkeeping replayed in original order (identical values, identical callback sequence).
- **What stays synchronous.** The fragment-fill D2H (render_engine.cu:786-790) remains mid-eval in Cuts 1-2 — but in the batched design its wait overlaps the *previous* eval's already-enqueued kernels, so it stops being an idle bubble. Only Cut 3 removes it entirely.
- **Biplane overlap for free.** Keep the primary metrics' async copies outstanding while enqueuing the secondary Render + FastImplantDilationMetric (different camera buffers, default-stream order is safe); wait once at the end. No double-buffer needed for this one.
- **Streams vs. single stream.** Two explicit streams (copy stream for the D2H + compute stream for kernels, joined by events) are an optional refinement once events exist; the default-stream version captures most of the win with less risk. 04's architecture angle owns the broader backend shape; the seam here is only "eval state is double-buffered and the cost layer can enqueue before it waits."

* nvtx instrumentation plan

Ranges (nvtx3 header-only, `#include <nvtx3/nvtx3.hpp>`, no link/CMake change; compile in always, they are ~ns overhead):

- **Per-eval** (the range that makes the sync structure visible): wrap `CostFunctionManager::callActiveCostFunction` (src/compute/CostFunctionManager.cpp:276-298) or the cost lambda in `OptimizerManager::RunDirectStage` (optimizer_manager.cpp:1238-1248) — name it "eval", optionally annotate the stage (trunk/branch/leaf) via `nvtx3::scoped_range`.
- **Per-stage within an eval**: `RenderEngine::Render` (render_engine.cu:711), `GPUMetrics::FastImplantDilationMetric` (fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:169), `GPUMetrics::DistanceMapMetric` (distance_map_metric.cu:71).
- **Per-iteration**: the DirectOptimizer `Run` loop body (direct_optimizer.cpp:41-49) — this makes the batch boundary visible once Cut 2 lands.
- **Per-frame**: `OptimizerManager::Optimize` frame-loop body (optimizer_manager.cpp:970-1050 region; the frame loop sets budgets at :991-993) — name it "frame N".
- **Per-sync markers**: `nvtx3::mark` immediately before each of the 5 D2H copies (render_engine.cu:781,786; fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:289; distance_map_metric.cu:110,115) so Nsight shows exactly which sync drains what.

Tooling: `ncu` (nsight-compute 2024.1) is already in the environment for kernel-level data (FillTriangleKernel, DilateKernel, DistanceMapMetric_Kernel); `nsys` (Nsight Systems) must be added (`pixi add nsight-systems`) or used from the system. Capture: `nsys profile --trace=cuda,nvtx --cuda-memory-usage=true .build/bin/jtml_test_oracle` run under a small eval budget, then a production-budget capture of a single frame. Headless default is preserved: instrumentation is inside jtml_compute and inert without a profiler attached.

* Measurement protocol (first profiling run)

1. **Event-based per-eval wall clock** in `test/oracle/oracle_test.cpp`: `cudaEventRecord` start/stop around `p.trunk->callActiveCostFunction()` inside the DirectOptimizer cost lambda (oracle_test.cpp:286-290), accumulating per-eval mean/p50/p95 across the budget. Record the same for `Render()` alone, `FastImplantDilationMetric` alone, `DistanceMapMetric` alone.
2. **Compare against the clock() meter** (optimizer_manager.cpp:1274): capture both simultaneously in a harness run; quantify the gap. Expect event-time > clock()-time whenever syncs or kernels dominate — that gap is the proof of the item-8 claim's magnitude.
3. **Nsight Systems trace** (with the nvtx ranges above): per-eval breakdown = kernel time (sum of ~15 kernel spans) vs. sync stall (gaps between the last kernel before each D2H and the first kernel after the wait) vs. driver/launch overhead. The decisive number: total GPU-active time per eval vs. total wall time per eval.
4. **Nsight Compute** on FillTriangleKernel and DilateKernel: confirm they are memory/latency-bound small kernels (no hidden fat kernel), which justifies treating kernel time as roughly irreducible and sync time as the target.
5. **Bit-identity harness**: a recorded fixed pose sequence (e.g. first 1000 evals of the oracle's frame 0) dumped as (pose → cost) pairs; re-run after each cut and diff — must be identical (int-atomic reductions make this achievable; see determinism finding).
6. **Gate structure for every cut**: (a) headless suite green (`pixi run test`), (b) oracle green (IoU ≥ 0.85 on all 3 frames, oracle_test.cpp:245,333; TIMEOUT 3600 in test/CMakeLists.txt:1253), (c) bit-identity diff empty where claimed, (d) measured per-eval event-time improvement ≥ the cut's predicted Δ (a cut that doesn't move the needle gets reverted — measure-first discipline).

* Ordered cuts with gates

** Cut 0 — Instrument (no behavior change). nvtx3 ranges + event timing + nsys/ncu capture + baseline table. Gate: baseline recorded (per-eval kernel time vs sync stall vs launch overhead; clock()-meter vs event-meter gap). Nothing to regress.

** Cut 1 — Async terminal copies + one event wait per eval (cheapest, highest win-per-risk). Convert the 3 terminal D2H (fast_implant_dilation_metric.cu:289-290; distance_map_metric.cu:110-119) to `cudaMemcpyAsync` into the existing pinned buffers + `cudaEventRecord`/`cudaEventSynchronize` at the eval boundary; fold in the stray `cudaGetLastError()` deletion (render_engine.cu:713). Net effect: 3 sync round trips become 1 event wait; the distance-map pair shares one drain with the fast-implant score; the copies overlap each other and the kernels' tails. Gate: oracle green; per-eval event-time down by measured Δ; bit-identity diff empty. Expected: removes ~2 of 3 drain windows per eval + 2-3 driver round trips — likely 10-40% of per-eval wall time, pending Cut 0 numbers.

** Cut 2 — Iteration batching + double-buffered eval state (the streamed pipeline; no kernel rewrites). DirectOptimizer batch surface (collect iteration poses → enqueue all evals back-to-back on alternating buffers → one terminal wait → replay bookkeeping in original order); second render output + duplicate dev score buffers. The mid-eval fragment sync stays but its wait now overlaps the previous eval's tail. Gate: oracle green; optimum pose + cost values bit-identical to a baseline run of the same seed/budget (callback replay order preserves behavior); per-eval event-time drops further. This is the user's "per-eval sync removal" in its strongest non-kernel form.

** Cut 3 — Remove the fragment-fill mid-eval sync (the one kernel-level change; conditional). Only if Cut 0-2 leave render_engine.cu:786-790 as the dominant remaining stall. Mechanics: clamp the guards in StridePrefixKernel (render_engine.cu:812-813) and FillTriangleKernel (:823-824) to `min(fragment_fill, SAFE_CAP)` with SAFE_CAP = maximum_stride_size * threads_per_block, so the stride-prefix buffer can never be written out of bounds; launch those two kernels with a fixed grid sized from a per-model worst-case bound; move the overflow check to a deferred async read (frame aborts at detection — the current behavior is already abort-the-frame, render_engine.cu:795-808). Bit-identity: threads `< fragment_fill` must do exactly today's work (extra threads exit at the guard; no writes, no shared-memory init change). Gate: oracle green; non-overflow renders bit-identical; overflow frames still error the frame. If the analytic worst-case grid is unacceptable (fragment count is pose-dependent and can exceed any fixed bound), keep the sync and accept it as the one structural cost.

** Cut 4 — Fix the meter (optimizer_manager.cpp:1272-1278). Replace `clock()` with a wall-clock (std::chrono::steady_clock for host-side, cudaEvent for GPU-inclusive) so ms/call includes GPU + sync time. Gate: meter tracks the event-measured per-eval time within noise. This is required before any of Cuts 1-3 can be *demonstrated* to the user via the UI meter.

** Biplane note (free win, fold into Cut 1): with async terminal copies, the primary metrics' D2H overlaps the secondary Render kernels (separate buffers, gpu_model.cu:144-146) with no double-buffering — wait once at the end of costFunctionDIRECT_DILATION's biplane branch.

** CPU fallback for Tier-0 — recommend against. The headless Tier-0 suite is already CUDA-free by construction: DirectOptimizer is pure (direct_optimizer.h:11-13 "zero Qt/VTK/CUDA/JTML dependencies") and tested with injected costs (test/CMakeLists.txt:46-63, 86-97); cost-parameter logic has deterministic twins (test/CMakeLists.txt:236-265). The GPU cost path's only gate is the `oracle` label (test/CMakeLists.txt:1150-1254), which is exactly what Cuts 0-3 make GPU-CI-tractable. A CPU rasterizer + dilation port is a separate large project with no current consumer; if CPU-side coverage of the cost *math* is wanted, that belongs to 02's metric-math tests (host-side reference implementations), not a render engine port.

* What Could Not Be Verified

- Actual per-eval kernel times, sync-stall latencies, and the kernel-vs-sync split — requires Cut 0 on the RTX 3090 (oracle machine). The item-8 claim's *magnitude* is unverified; only its structural plausibility is confirmed.

Headless-verifiable determinism argument: the replay contract is pure domain logic and testable without a GPU — a Tier-0 test (test/unit/test_direct_optimizer family) with a scripted batch cost asserts: (a) the batch callback receives exactly the pose sequence the sequential path evaluates (recorded from a sequential reference run on the same seed), (b) after Run(), the storage (DirectDataStorage columns/values), optimum location/value, GetCostFunctionCalls(), and the improvement/iteration callback sequences are identical between the sequential and batched paths fed the same scripted values. GPU-side bit-identity: identical kernels, launch configs, and stream order per eval; only host-wait interleaving changes; int-atomics ⇒ same scores. Verified by the pose→score diff harness on the oracle.

Prediction: after Cut 1, the per-eval host-block is the render drain + the terminal wait; batching hides both behind the previous eval's GPU work. Predicted Δ = the measured host-block-window sum from Cut 0 minus what Cut 1 already removed. Gate: headless green (incl. the new Tier-0 batch test), oracle green, bit-identity empty, per-eval event-time reduction ≥ prediction. Revert rule: if the batched path shows no improvement (or a regression) over 3 runs, abandon the jj change and keep sequential.

### Cut 3 — fragment-fill removal: the decision procedure (conditional)

Trigger measurement (during Cut 0): the fragment sweep (fragment_fill_[0] min/max/p99/max-ever + bbox per eval over frame-0's 3000 evals) plus the render-drain time (event gap from PrepareLaunchPacketKernel completion to the fill kernels' start).

Trigger condition (BOTH must hold; pre-registered from Cut 0's data):

(a) the render drain (bbox+fragment sync + overflow check + launch latency) is the dominant remaining per-eval stall after Cuts 1-2 — e.g., ≥ 50% of per-eval wall (number fixed from Cut 0's table);
(b) the fragment distribution is tightly bounded: max_observed × margin < SAFE_CAP = maximum_stride_size × threads_per_block = 2.55e9 (the capacity ceiling, R2-3), AND a GRID_CAP/256-block launch is affordable (measure the empty-grid launch time for the chosen GRID_CAP — the analytic ceiling would be ~10M blocks, so the practical GRID_CAP comes from the measured distribution, e.g., next power-of-two ≥ max_observed × 2).

Device-side clamp design (R2-3 makes it a host-side change): compute `fill = min(fragment_fill_[0], GRID_CAP)`; launch StridePrefixKernel and FillTriangleKernel from `fill` (ceil(fill/(256×256)) and ceil(fill/256) — the existing launch expressions at render_engine.cu:812-816/:823-826 with the value substituted). Optionally clamp on-device (PrepareLaunchPacketKernel writes min(fragment_fill, GRID_CAP) to a second device int) so the host never needs the true value to launch. NO kernel-source change: threads/blocks beyond the true total exit at the existing in-kernel guards (StridePrefixKernel :592-593; FillTriangleKernel :628-629, which wraps the whole body including the shared-mem load + __syncthreads :636-641), writing nothing. Non-overflow renders are bit-identical by construction (threads < total do exactly today's work).

Overflow semantics preserved (non-negotiable): if fragment_fill_[0] > GRID_CAP, the eval must NOT silently under-render (fragments in (GRID_CAP, total) would never be processed). Two safe behaviors: (i) per-eval fallback to the synchronous read + dynamic grid (the current path — keep the sync as the tail handler), or (ii) abort the frame exactly as today (fragment_overflow_ = true + cudaErrorMemoryAllocation, render_engine.cu:795-808). The fallback keeps bit-identity for all non-fallback evals and preserves error behavior for the tail. The bbox sync (:781-785) is NOT touched by Cut 3 (the crop/grid host math still needs it).

Safe fallback (the decision's default): if (a) or (b) fails — unbounded tail, or GRID_CAP blocks unaffordable — keep the fragment sync and accept it as the one structural cost; in the batched pipeline (Cut 2) its wait already overlaps the previous eval's tail, so the remaining exposure is small. This is a measured no-go, not a punt.

Prediction: Δ = the measured render-drain sum minus the residual fallback cost. Gate: oracle green, non-overflow bit-identity empty, overflow frames still error, event-time reduction ≥ prediction.

### Cut 4 — the event-based ms/call meter (full spec)

Replace BOTH clock() meters: optimizer_manager.cpp:1272-1279 (RunDirectStage iteration callback — the dispatch's :1274-1281) and :1197-1203 (end-of-frame emit). Both currently compute CPU-ticks/call (µs on Linux) and emit it as "ms/call" — CPU-only, GPU-blind, sync-blind, and 1000× unit-wrong (R2-1).

New meter spec:

- wall ms/call = std::chrono::steady_clock elapsed over the stage (RunDirectStage entry → current iteration callback) / opt.GetCostFunctionCalls() — wall INCLUDES GPU time and sync-wait time (the host blocks inside the driver), satisfying "includes GPU time".
- GPU ms/call = the cudaEvent per-eval deltas from Cut 0's instrumentation, accumulated per stage — logged alongside (or the meter owns one minimal event pair per stage if instrumentation is compiled out). wall − GPU = host overhead + sync stalls, reported so the item-8 claim stays visible in the UI's data trail.
- Units: emit TRUE ms/call. The existing UI math then becomes correct without UI changes: "Iterations Per Second: 1000.0 / iteration_speed" (view/mainscreen.cpp:4654-4655) and the ETA (:4598/:4659) both assume ms/call. The fix is at the meter, not the UI.
- Where the UI reads it (verified): UpdateDisplay(double iteration_speed, ...) → OptimizerRunController::onManagerUpdateDisplay (coordinator/optimizer_run_controller.cpp:243) → updateDisplayRelayed → MainScreen::onUpdateDisplay (view/mainscreen.cpp:4582; speed :4654-4655, ETA :4598/:4659, VTK actor text). The QML/experimental path (OptimizerBridge.h) relays no speed today (R2-2) — adding it is a separate small change if the QML UI needs the meter.
- No behavior change to the search. Gate: meter tracks the event-measured per-eval time within noise (wall ≥ event always; the gap is reported, not asserted).

### The measurement protocol every cut must pass

For Cuts 1-3 (Cut 4 is meter-only; Cut 0 is record-only):

(a) headless green — pixi run test (ctest -L headless, --timeout 600; the batch cut adds its Tier-0 replay test to this set);
(b) oracle green — ctest --test-dir .build -L oracle → jtml.oracle: IoU > 0.85 per frame (oracle_test.cpp:333; kIouGate :245, kBudget 3000 :244, TIMEOUT 3600 at test/CMakeLists.txt:1253). Runs only after the synthesis step-1 re-baseline so the gate compares against the trustworthy baseline;
(c) bit-identity diff empty — the pose→score recorder harness: the first 1000 evals of oracle frame 0 recorded as (pose, cost) pairs (recorder at the oracle cost lambda, oracle_test.cpp:288-291); diff vs the baseline recording after each cut. Empty where the cut claims bit-identity (Cuts 1, 2; Cut 3 on non-overflow evals);
(d) measured improvement ≥ prediction — each cut pre-registers its predicted Δ from Cut 0's table (Cut 1: converted-sync stall sum; Cut 2: host-block window sum; Cut 3: render-drain sum); acceptance = mean per-eval event-time reduction over the same 3000-eval sequence ≥ prediction, reproducible over 3 runs.

Revert rule: a cut that measures < prediction (or a regression) is reverted in the same jj change (jj abandon) with the measurement recorded in the run's artifacts; the cut may be retried only with a new prediction derived from the new baseline. Cuts land in order 0 → 1 → 2 → 4 → (3 conditional) — Cut 3 never before Cut 2, Cut 4 before any cut is demonstrated to the user via the UI.

- The actual fragment_fill_ distribution and render-drain times — need the GPU sweep on the RTX 3090 (Cut 0, record item 8). Cut 3's go/no-go is unmeasured until then.
- Whether nvtx3 resolves in the coordinator TUs (include-path question — verify at build; the additive toolkit-include fallback is specified).
- The empty-grid launch cost of a large fixed GRID_CAP (measure at Cut 3 trigger time; the analytic ceiling of ~10M blocks is schedulable but plausibly ms-scale).
- Whether cudaEventSynchronize per eval (Cut 1) still pays a meaningful driver wake-up on this driver/arch — the measurement decides whether Cut 2's restructuring is justified.
- The user-visible magnitude of the R2-1 unit bug (the code path is verified; the numbers on the user's display were not captured).
- GPUMetrics' SetActiveBank semantics vs the three per-stage CFMs sharing one instance (the stage loop is sequential so no interleave by construction, but the invariant is asserted, not yet tested).

#+TITLE: Panoptes Research: Optimizer Deep-Dive — Architecture + Algorithm Upgrades
#+DATE: 2026-08-12
#+RESEARCH_ANGLES: 6
#+ROUND: 3 (wave 1 complete) — angles 01–04 carry '## Round 3' sections grounded in Zotero primary texts; angles 05–06 remain round-2 complete (rounds: 1 = all six; 2 wave 1 = 01–04; 2 wave 2 = 05–06; 3 wave 1 = 01–04)
#+STATUS: complete

* Executive Summary

The single highest-leverage finding of this run: **the current 0.9936 IoU baseline is measured against a deterministically-corrupted cost term.** Angle 02 verified at the dispatch's line numbers that the distance-map index formula (distance_map_metric.cu:27, `blockIdx.y + gridDim.x` instead of `blockIdx.y * gridDim.x`) mis-maps every block row, so the distance-map term of every DIRECT_DILATION oracle evaluation accumulates at the wrong pixels. That is the one live bug of the seven verified — the other six poison latent paths only. Fixing it and re-baselining (one single re-baseline after all behavior-neutral fixes land) is the prerequisite for every other decision in this run: variant switches, perf cuts, and gradient polish are all judged against a baseline that is not trustworthy until this lands. The gate (IoU ≥ 0.85) is far below the measured 0.9936, so the appearance arbiter stays, but measured IoU / per-px L1 / the 6.31 mm z gap are informational and expected to move.

Round 2 sharpened the critical path in an important way: the corrupted index has **exactly one reader** (DistanceMapMetric_Kernel, invoked only from DIRECT_DILATION.cpp:80), and every post-optimize measurement metric (IoU, per-px L1, chamfer) uses the correct formula — so the 0.9936/0.0207 numbers themselves are not corrupted, only the cost that drove the search. The corruption is a systematic exclusion: the top ~64 crop rows of the rendered band are never sampled and the middle band is multiplicity-over-weighted, so the distance-map term is *flatter in z* than the honest chamfer complement. The structural prediction is that the re-baselined DIRECT optimum moves toward the golden z and the frame-1 6.31 mm z gap shrinks materially (direction: medium-high confidence; magnitude: not predictable without the GPU re-run).

Round 2 wave 2 added two more high-value deliverables on top of the wave-1 deepening. **First, the ms/call meter carries a 1000× unit error on Linux, on top of its CPU-time blind spot**: grep finds zero CLOCKS_PER_SEC anywhere in src/ — both meter sites (optimizer_manager.cpp:1197-1203 end-of-frame and :1272-1279 iteration callback) divide raw clock() ticks by calls and label the result "ms/call"; on Linux glibc clock() returns microseconds, so the value is CPU-µs/call labeled as ms/call. The UI compounds it: "Iterations Per Second: 1000.0 / iteration_speed" (mainscreen.cpp:4654-4655) reads the µs value as ms → IPS understated ~1000×, and the ETA (:4598/:4659) is overstated by the same factor. This is a correctness fact, not polish — no before/after perf claim through the existing meter is meaningful, and Cut 4 (now a full spec for BOTH sites) must emit true ms/call so the existing UI math becomes correct without UI changes. [Source: angles/05-compute-perf.org R2-1/R2-2] **Second, the polish stage is now an executable MVP spec with its own falsifiable preconditions**: a term-decomposed z-profile probe (chamfer-only vs dilated-overlap-only valley depths from the same 31 renders, pre-registered thresholds G1–G4 at leaf dilation 1), a forward-difference arm (7 renders/accepted step, ~140 steps within B_p = 1000), an analytic arm (1 render/step via the 2×6 projection Jacobian + gradient-of-distance-map kernel, with an ordered two-pass float reduction so the ablation runner's rerun_identical determinism twin cannot trip), and a **three-arm study (A: DIRECT@35k, B: DIRECT@34k budget-gift control, C: DIRECT@34k + polish@1000)** that arbitrates the 12x-vs-1.5–3x contradiction without confounding "polish quality" with "budget reallocation". [Source: angles/06-differentiable-polish.org R2-1/R2-2/R2-4/R2-5]

Round 3 (wave 1) moved the run's evidentiary base onto the primary texts: angles 01–04 re-verified their round-1/2 conclusions against the Zotero corpus (Flood 2018, Mahfouz 2003, Jones 1993, Gablonsky 2001, Jensen 2024, Yamazaki 2004, the DIRECTGO / DIRECT-GLh / 2022-study papers, Burton, Arulampalam) and **resolved three open contradictions outright**. (1) **Mahfouz normalization**: the paper corroborates the kernel's structure (two predicted-sum-normalized ratios, contour weighted more heavily, negative weights, a 3-px capture band — a full lineage match) but the numeric weights are unextractable (embedded PDF equations), so the kernel-as-spec verdict keeps 2.55/×255/−2.67/−1 and only the pointer-guard fix proceeds. (2) **Three-way dilation contradiction**: Flood's constants are now verbatim — femur 10/6/1, tibia 6/2/1, branch = trunk−4, leaf = 1; leaf=1 is unanimous, trunk 6 (code AND docs) is the paper's TIBIA value applied to a FEMUR (femur robust band 8–12), and BOTH 6/4/1 and 6/3/1 violate branch=trunk−4 — so the dilation-schedule ablation now tests the lineage configs {10,6,1}, {6,2,1}, {6,4,1}, {6,3,1} plus a bilateral-vs-render-only semantics axis. (3) **GLh formula**: verified from the paper itself (raw surrogate f_min + d stored, selection-time normalized d̃ = d/√n with f̃_min ≡ 0, f̃=1 flat case, 1e-6 recompute threshold, Definition-1 feasibility detection) with a ready-made constrained battery (Emmental-GKLS, 100/100 solved by GLh in the paper). * Executive Summary

The single highest-leverage finding of this run: **the current 0.9936 IoU baseline is measured against a deterministically-corrupted cost term.** Angle 02 verified at the dispatch's line numbers that the distance-map index formula (distance_map_metric.cu:27, `blockIdx.y + gridDim.x` instead of `blockIdx.y * gridDim.x`) mis-maps every block row, so the distance-map term of every DIRECT_DILATION oracle evaluation accumulates at the wrong pixels. That is the one live bug of the seven verified — the other six poison latent paths only. Fixing it and re-baselining (one single re-baseline after all behavior-neutral fixes land) is the prerequisite for every other decision in this run: variant switches, perf cuts, and gradient polish are all judged against a baseline that is not trustworthy until this lands. The gate (IoU ≥ 0.85) is far below the measured 0.9936, so the appearance arbiter stays, but measured IoU / per-px L1 / the 6.31 mm z gap are informational and expected to move.

Round 2 sharpened the critical path in an important way: the corrupted index has **exactly one reader** (DistanceMapMetric_Kernel, invoked only from DIRECT_DILATION.cpp:80), and every post-optimize measurement metric (IoU, per-px L1, chamfer) uses the correct formula — so the 0.9936/0.0207 numbers themselves are not corrupted, only the cost that drove the search. The corruption is a systematic exclusion: the top ~64 crop rows of the rendered band are never sampled and the middle band is multiplicity-over-weighted, so the distance-map term is *flatter in z* than the honest chamfer complement. The structural prediction is that the re-baselined DIRECT optimum moves toward the golden z and the frame-1 6.31 mm z gap shrinks materially (direction: medium-high confidence; magnitude: not predictable without the GPU re-run).

Round 2 wave 2 added two more high-value deliverables on top of the wave-1 deepening. **First, the ms/call meter carries a 1000× unit error on Linux, on top of its CPU-time blind spot**: grep finds zero CLOCKS_PER_SEC anywhere in src/ — both meter sites (optimizer_manager.cpp:1197-1203 end-of-frame and :1272-1279 iteration callback) divide raw clock() ticks by calls and label the result "ms/call"; on Linux glibc clock() returns microseconds, so the value is CPU-µs/call labeled as ms/call. The UI compounds it: "Iterations Per Second: 1000.0 / iteration_speed" (mainscreen.cpp:4654-4655) reads the µs value as ms → IPS understated ~1000×, and the ETA (:4598/:4659) is overstated by the same factor. This is a correctness fact, not polish — no before/after perf claim through the existing meter is meaningful, and Cut 4 (now a full spec for BOTH sites) must emit true ms/call so the existing UI math becomes correct without UI changes. [Source: angles/05-compute-perf.org R2-1/R2-2] **Second, the polish stage is now an executable MVP spec with its own falsifiable preconditions**: a term-decomposed z-profile probe (chamfer-only vs dilated-overlap-only valley depths from the same 31 renders, pre-registered thresholds G1–G4 at leaf dilation 1), a forward-difference arm (7 renders/accepted step, ~140 steps within B_p = 1000), an analytic arm (1 render/step via the 2×6 projection Jacobian + gradient-of-distance-map kernel, with an ordered two-pass float reduction so the ablation runner's rerun_identical determinism twin cannot trip), and a **three-arm study (A: DIRECT@35k, B: DIRECT@34k budget-gift control, C: DIRECT@34k + polish@1000)** that arbitrates the 12x-vs-1.5–3x contradiction without confounding "polish quality" with "budget reallocation". [Source: angles/06-differentiable-polish.org R2-1/R2-2/R2-4/R2-5]

Round 3 (wave 1) moved the run's evidentiary base onto the primary texts: angles 01–04 re-verified their round-1/2 conclusions against the Zotero corpus (Flood 2018, Mahfouz 2003, Jones 1993, Gablonsky 2001, Jensen 2024, Yamazaki 2004, the DIRECTGO / DIRECT-GLh / 2022-study papers, Burton, Arulampalam) and **resolved three open contradictions outright**. (1) **Mahfouz normalization**: the paper corroborates the kernel's structure (two predicted-sum-normalized ratios, contour weighted more heavily, negative weights, a 3-px capture band — a full lineage match) but the numeric weights are unextractable (embedded PDF equations), so the kernel-as-spec verdict keeps 2.55/×255/−2.67/−1 and only the pointer-guard fix proceeds. Two tensions the user should carry explicitly. First, **the variant switch cannot fix the z-axis**: the variant choice (search scheme) and the z-sensitivity ranking (cost observability) are orthogonal in mechanism, with only two documented second-order interactions (the NaN/Inf trigger and refinement-control savings on z-flat costs); the harness must report evals and z-error separately, and a variant-switch win must never be read as a z fix. Round 3 adds the lineage's own confirmation: Flood's success metric excludes z by definition ("out-of-plane translation is not considered in our definition of success"), the z-stage exists explicitly "because it is the least accurate degree of freedom for single-plane fluoroscopy", and the field's z-accuracy band (Yamazaki 2.6–3.2 mm conventional → 0.9–1.8 mm remedied; Jensen out-of-plane < 1.8 mm; Arulampalam depth MAE 1.8 mm) frames JTML's measured 6.31 mm as a candidate regression — the multi-stage oracle and probe are the instruments that decide. Second, **perf cuts do not sacrifice determinism**: every active cost-path reduction is an int atomicAdd (order-independent, value-deterministic), so async copies and iteration batching can preserve bit-identical results; angle 04's seam contract pins the double-buffered eval state, and the polish gradient must use an ordered (non-atomic) float reduction because the ablation runner's rerun_identical determinism twin would trip on float-atomic accumulation.

Round 2 also closed the run's longest-standing open question: **the DIRECT-GLh NaN trigger is now resolved per-variant.** DIRECT_DILATION is structurally incapable of emitting NaN/Inf (all-int composition, +0.1-guarded division, max accumulation 2.55e8 ≪ 2³¹) — the GLh trigger lives in DIRECT_MAHFOUZ (0/0 via the pointer-guard bug, production-reachable), DD_NEW_POLE_CONSTRAINT (UB min_dist), and sym_trap (asin domain). The finite-check belongs at the one shared chokepoint, DirectOptimizer::EvaluateCostFunction (direct_optimizer.cpp:205), and the round-1 claim that "NaN poisons hull slope comparisons" is corrected: NaN boxes accumulate as dead weight at the column front (lost evals, unbounded growth), with the column minimum poisoned only after all finite boxes are trisected away — a delayed, conditional effect, still worth closing. Round 3's Mahfouz paper read adds no new emitter information but corroborates the metric's structure (and its SA-modified Nelder-Mead optimizer, from which the repo deliberately diverged). The "12x fewer evals" polish thesis remains a target to test, not a justification: angle 06's analysis puts the realistic win at ~1.5–3× in the leaf/refinement phase, with the chamfer distance-map surrogate as the one smooth gradient signal — and wave 2's three-arm study is the instrument that will measure it. Everything else from the papers — 1-DTDV boundary sampling, analytic-AA occlusion gradients, DRR-photometric gradients, torch bridges — stays conditional, deferred, or NO-GO, and each lands only through the harness.

A. Convergence Testing
To determine the furthest distance from the true pose at
which DIRECT-JTA can consistently converge using ideal
constants, we began by collecting 40 fluoroscopic images from
two studies on stair stepping motion cycles at a capture rate
of 30 frames per second with a resolution of approximately
0.75 megapixels and a density of .255 mm per pixel edge.
Patients had been fitted with either GMK Sphere implants from
Medacta International SA, Switzerland (Group A) or 3DKnee
implants from DJO Surgical, Austin, Texas (Group B). Note
each patient received two implants (one femoral and one tibial)
leading to a total of four cases: Group A femoral/tibial and
Group B femoral/tibial. After removing images where one or
more of the implants were not fully in frame, ten images
were randomly selected from each study. 100 random poses
(ten per image) were subsequently generated for each of the
four implant models at a specified maximum displacement
range. We evaluated the algorithm for the femoral implants at
±25, ±35, ±45, and ±55 mm/degrees for each of the six pose
components using independent Uniform distributions across
the given ranges. Tibial implants were studied using ranges
of ±25, ±30, ±35, and ±40 mm/degrees. This meant that
each model group had 400 unique starting poses for a total
of 1,600 trial runs. The performance of the algorithm was
measured by three metrics: strict success rate, relaxed success
rate, and the average convergence error from the baseline data
of strict successes. The strict success rate is the percentage
of random poses that DIRECT-JTA moved to within 1 mm
for each of the in-plane translations and 1 degree for each
of the rotation angles. Accuracy within ±1 mm/degree provides clinically usable information about joint kinematics [10],
therefore we use this threshold as our margin of tolerance.
However, this does not necessarily mean that strict success
rate is a measure of clinical tolerance (for further discussion
please see the concluding section of the article). The relaxed
rate expands these boundaries to ±3 mm/degrees in order to
gauge the ability of the algorithm to generate a close attempt.
Note that out-of-plane translation is not considered in our
definition of success. The motivation for this exclusion stems
from the fact that single-plane, or monocular, radiographic
images are extremely unreliable for determining out-of-plane
position [10]; this is expected as the translation occurs along
the line of sight. An orthogonal biplane comparison is likely
the best resolution for this inaccuracy. It should be noted that
differences in the registration success rates between groups are
certainly not an indicator of implant quality. Each group also
used different imaging devices which contributed to a slightly
better contrast between the surrounding tissue/bone and the
implants in Group B than in Group A.

331

Successful convergence of a black-box optimization problem is largely dependent on the complexity of the cost function
and the size of the search range. Although in radiographic
model-image registration each X-ray/implant pair has a unique
similarity mapping, function complexity varies primarily with
image noise and model type. This situation implies that the
difficulty of finding the optimum pose for an implant is
relatively consistent across an image sequence because the
quality of images and intricacy of the silhouettes are generally
the same (notable exceptions include an out-of-frame implant
and interference from metallic objects).

B. Algorithm Constants
Like most optimization routines, the correct specification
of the algorithm parameters was important to the success of
DIRECT-JTA. Through trial and error the high-performance
values for the dilation level (in pixels) and the Canny edge
detector values were determined for each of the four cases.
Significant effort was made to ensure the values for these
constants were as general as possible, however a sensitivity
analysis was also undertaken in a later section. The two other
constants, iteration count and search range size, were set in
accordance with available computing power and experiment
pose displacement, respectively.
Both femur groups were set at dilation levels of 10 for
the trunk search stage, while the tibia groups used a dilation
level of 6. In all four cases, the dilation was decreased by
a value of four in the branch search stage, and the final
z-search stage was conducted at a dilation level of one. The
Canny edge detection algorithm was used to remove noise
from the biological materials, whilst retaining the edges of the
implants. Using a fixed value of three for the aperture size of
the Sobel operator (higher values led to unacceptable levels of
interference) the threshold values for both implants in Group B
and the tibial implants in Group A were set to 40 and 120.
The femoral implants in Group A needed threshold values of
30 and 80 in order to display similar levels of clarity to the
other implants.
Iteration count for the algorithm was pegged to take approximately one minute of operating time. The iteration budget
was 50,000 for the trunk search, 15,000 for each of the three
branch searches, and 50,000 for the z-translation search. Using
a 4GHz Intel Core i7 4790K in conjunction with a Nvidia
GeForce GTX 970, a GPU based version of the registration
routine achieved speeds of approximately 3,000 iterations per
second (50 seconds per frame).
The trunk search range sizes were set to the search range
being tested, while the branch restart sizes were 15 mm for
the in-plane translation, 25 mm for the out-of-plane translation,
and 25° for each of the Euler angles. This allowed the branch
search to easily overcome local minima that the highly dilated
trunk search had identified due to symmetry. The in-plane
translation components were set slightly smaller than the
rest as the algorithm typically found good values for the
x and y translation rather quickly. During the z-translation
search phase the out-of-plane range was set to 20 mm while
all other components were set to 5 mm/degrees.

Tables I - IV display the the success rates and the average
convergence error of successful registrations for each of the
four groups. The femoral implants performed extremely well
through the ± 55 test set, with near perfect success rates and
an average out-of-plane translation around one millimeter. The
Group A tibial implants were similarly excellent at all ranges
tested, however, the Group B set saw a sharp drop off for the
strict success rate after the ± 25 search range. This was largely
due to the highly symmetric nature of the tibial implant’s
position in many of the frames, which created a deep local

minimum just over a degree along the Y Euler angle from
the optimum. The relaxed success rate proved to be far more
robust, although it also tapered off after the ± 35 search range.
It should be noted that this data set also contained significant
obstruction from the femoral implant leading to a reduction
in the detectable tibial edges (although this problem did not
seem to affect the femoral implant’s convergence range).

implants. Using a fixed value of three for the aperture size of
the Sobel operator (higher values led to unacceptable levels of
interference) the threshold values for both implants in Group B
and the tibial implants in Group A were set to 40 and 120.

30 and 80 in order to display similar levels of clarity to the
other implants.

branch searches, and 50,000 for the z-translation search. Using
a 4GHz Intel Core i7 4790K in conjunction with a Nvidia
GeForce GTX 970, a GPU based version of the registration
routine achieved speeds of approximately 3,000 iterations per
second (50 seconds per frame).

being tested, while the branch restart sizes were 15 mm for
the in-plane translation, 25 mm for the out-of-plane translation,

trunk search had identified due to symmetry. The in-plane
