arguments.content:
## Round 3

### Summary

The corpus's rendering/DRR evidence turns the cross-era throughput datum into a full, falsifiable baseline and gives the cut order its first external anchors. Flood 2018 (floodAutomatedRegistration3D2018.txt) is verified end-to-end as the sanity baseline: 145,000 evals (50k trunk + 3×15k branch + 50k z) at ~3,000 iterations/s = 333 µs per eval on a GTX 970 (the paper's own arithmetic checks: 145,000/3,000 ≈ 48 s ≈ "50 seconds per frame"), where the eval is deliberately GPU-cheap ("a simple L1 norm... can be computed by a GPU extremely efficiently" — render + one L1 pass, no chamfer, no per-eval input dilation). Abdellah 2015 measured the SAME GTX 970 rendering volumetric DRRs at 25 ms/2048² and 67 ms/4096² — so a silhouette eval is ~2 orders of magnitude cheaper than a volumetric DRR on identical silicon, and JTML's derived 16–50 ms/eval on an RTX 3090 (4.2× bandwidth, ~9× FP32) sits squarely in volumetric-DRR territory while doing silhouette work: the cross-era arithmetic implies ~95%+ of JTML's per-eval wall is host-side, a pre-registration Cut 0 can falsify (GPU-active per-eval > 1 ms inverts the cut order). The fast-DRR family licenses almost nothing for the fragment-fill rasterizer itself — bindless textures accelerate reads on volumetric cudaArrays, not the scatter-writes of a linear-memory fill (render_engine.cu:628-700); block projection (Mu 2016) and splatting are approximate-reuse techniques that break the run's bit-identity/determinism contract; CUDA/OpenGL interop is display-only. The real transfers are: Dorgham's "similarity on the GPU" doctrine — the primary-text antecedent of Cuts 1–3, with a measured ~2 ms CPU-similarity ≈ D2H-copy parity; Flood's own batch-render future-work note (L761–765) — the antecedent of Cut 2, verbatim; the field's sampled/reduced-resolution DRR evidence (registration-accuracy-preserving at 50% compression, failing at 75%) — the spec for a render-resolution ablation arm beyond the cuts; and Tornai's block-size data (10–145% swings) — a zero-semantics knob for Cut 0's ncu pass. Pre-registered evals/s on the 3090: today 20–60 (derived), Cut 1 → 60–300, Cut 2 → 1,000–5,000 with Flood's 3,000 evals/s as the cross-era parity line; Cut 4's meter fix gains a wall-clock cross-check gate.

### Key Findings (Round 3)

#### R3-1 — Flood 2018 is the sanity baseline, verified verbatim (arithmetic + cost semantics)

- Budget and speed (floodAutomatedRegistration3D2018.txt L568–574): "The iteration budget was 50,000 for the trunk search, 15,000 for each of the three branch searches, and 50,000 for the z-translation search. Using a 4GHz Intel Core i7 4790K in conjunction with a Nvidia GeForce GTX 970, a GPU based version of the registration routine achieved speeds of approximately 3,000 iterations per second (50 seconds per frame)." Arithmetic check: 145,000/3,000 = 48.3 s ≈ "50 seconds per frame" — "iteration" = cost-function eval; per-eval = 333 µs INCLUDING DIRECT bookkeeping on the host.
- Cost semantics (L157–162): "The score is a simple L1 norm that rewards matching edges and punishes overlapping black space. There is no need for normalization because we are interested in finding the global minimum... We use L1 in place of other p-norms because it can be computed by a graphics processing unit (GPU) extremely efficiently." The eval = silhouette render + one L1 pass; the input Canny frame is dilated ONCE per stage (not per eval); there is NO chamfer/distance-map term and no per-eval input dilation — JTML's extra metric stages (fast-implant edge/dilate/difference + distance-map chamfer, ~7 kernels) are the workload delta vs Flood, not the render.
- Budget-by-time design (L568): "Iteration count for the algorithm was pegged to take approximately one minute of operating time." The lineage sizes budgets by WALL TIME; JTML's are fixed eval counts (20k/5k×2/5k). If the cuts raise evals/s toward Flood's rate, each frame gets faster in wall time without changing the search — a pure win — but the lineage's time-budget framing is a flag for the budget-constants conversation (they were tuned against a slow pipeline).
- Confidence: high (verbatim quotes; arithmetic verified). Relevance: this is the baseline the dispatch requires — the first nvtx/cudaEvent record must report JTML's per-eval time against 333 µs/eval (GTX 970, 2018).

#### R3-2 — Same-GPU cross-check: a volumetric DRR costs ~2 orders more than a silhouette eval on the identical GTX 970

- Abdellah 2015 (abdellahGPUAccelerationDigitally2015.txt L14–15, L333–337): bindless-texture + ray-march volumetric DRR pipeline on "an NVIDIA GeForce 970 GTX": "the pipeline line can generate 2048² and 4096² DRRs at 40 and 15 frames per second respectively" — i.e. 25 ms and 67 ms per volumetric DRR, versus Flood's 333 µs per silhouette+L1 eval on the same GPU: a 75–200× per-frame gap. This validates that the silhouette+L1 design is the field's cheap-cost choice and that JTML's fragment-fill renderer (also silhouette-based) belongs in the µs-per-eval regime, NOT the ms-per-eval regime.
- Cross-check corroboration: Tornai 2012 (tornaiFastDRRGeneration2012.txt L21–23) ray-cast DRR of a 400×225 ROI = 2.7–5.2 ms full-ROI (0.3–7.3 ms at 1.1–9.1% sampling) on 2007–2010 GPUs; Dorgham 2012 (dorghamGPUAcceleratedGeneration2012.txt L27–30) 256³ CT DRR ≈ 24 ms (8800 GTX) / ≈ 2 ms (GTX 580); Ikebe 2023 (ikebeDRRAccelerationUsing2023.txt L195–197, L424) Siddon–Jacobs DRR ≈ 61 ms on a laptop GTX 1650 Ti; Gopalakrishnan 2022 (gopalakrishnanFastAutoDifferentiableDigitally2022.txt L135–136) 200² DRR = 72.7 ms on an RTX 2080 Ti (PyTorch-vectorized — see R3-4 item 7). Volumetric DRRs are uniformly tens-of-ms; Flood's silhouette eval is sub-ms.
- Confidence: high (all numbers verbatim; the 75–200× ratio is arithmetic). Relevance: if Cut 0 measures JTML's per-eval wall in the tens-of-ms, the magnitude of the sync-bound claim is confirmed against the field's own per-eval economics; the comparison also quantifies how much headroom a GPU-only cost would have.

#### R3-3 — Cross-era arithmetic: JTML's derived 16–50 ms/eval on a ~9×-faster GPU implies ~95%+ host-block fraction (pre-registered, falsifiable)

- JTML today (derived, from the oracle's "a few minutes" for kBudget=3000; oracle_test.cpp:244): 20–60 evals/s → 16–50 ms/eval wall on the RTX 3090. Flood: 333 µs/eval on the GTX 970. Ratio: ~50–150× slower per eval on hardware ~3 generations newer.
- Hardware deltas (public specs): GTX 970 — 1,664 CUDA cores, 1.05/1.178 GHz, 224.4 GB/s, 3.92 TFLOPS FP32 (techpowerup.com/gpu-specs/geforce-gtx-970.c2620; nanoreview.net/en/gpu/geforce-gtx-970); RTX 3090 — 10,496 CUDA cores, 1.70 GHz boost, 24 GB GDDR6X, 936.2 GB/s, ~35.6 TFLOPS FP32 (nvidia.com/en-gb/geforce/graphics-cards/30-series/rtx-3090-3090ti/; techpowerup.com/gpu-specs/geforce-rtx-3090.c3622). Capability ratios for a fill/memory-bound workload: cores 6.3×, bandwidth 4.2×, FP32 ~9.1×.
- Workload adjustment: JTML's eval is heavier than Flood's (12,412-facet KR_right_7_fem.stl vs knee-implant models; +2 metric stages), but the 4–9× hardware advantage swamps a plausible 2–5× workload factor: the field-consistent GPU-active estimate for JTML's eval on the 3090 is ~50–500 µs (render: ~12k triangles → ~1–2M fragments → ~5–15 µs fill at 10,496 lanes + memset ~2 µs + projection/scan/launch ~30–75 µs; metrics over the ≤~500² crop ~10–50 µs). Even at the top of the band, 16–50 ms wall vs ~1 ms GPU-active ⇒ ≥ 95% of per-eval wall is host-block/driver/sync.
- FALSIFICATION pre-registration: if Cut 0's cudaEvent per-eval GPU-active measures > 1 ms on the 3090 (3× Flood's whole-eval on a 970), the sync-bound hypothesis fails in magnitude: the kernels themselves are then the problem and the order inverts to kernel-level work (ncu on FillTriangleKernel/DilateKernel/DistanceMapMetric_Kernel) BEFORE Cuts 1–2. If GPU-active is in the 50–500 µs band, Cuts 1–2 are validated as the correct lever and the post-Cut-2 wall should approach the GPU-active + launch-overhead floor.
- NEW contingency the corpus exposes: with ~15 launches/eval at ~2–5 µs driver overhead each, the per-eval floor after Cuts 1–2 is ~30–75 µs of launch overhead even with zero syncs — so the item-8 verdict can resolve into "launch-overhead-bound" rather than "sync-bound". That state is NOT addressed by Cut 3 (which removes one sync, not launches); the next lever would be a NEW direction: kernel fusion of the metric stage (FastImplantDilation + DistanceMap over the crop into one kernel — the "similarity on the GPU" doctrine of R3-5 applied to launches) as a Cut-5 candidate, pre-registered now, triggered if nsys shows launch gaps dominating post-Cut-2.
- Confidence: medium (JTML's 20–60 evals/s is itself derived from oracle runtimes and must be measured; hardware specs high; the GPU-active band is analytic, to be replaced by Cut 0). Relevance: this converts the round-1 "structurally confirmed, magnitude unmeasured" claim into a sharply falsifiable pre-registration with a numeric threshold.

#### R3-4 — Fast-DRR family vs the fragment-fill rasterizer (render_engine.cu): per-technique applicability verdicts

The JTML fill (FillTriangleKernel, render_engine.cu:616–700) is a fragment-scatter rasterizer: one thread per fragment of each triangle's pixel bbox, shared-memory binary search for the triangle index (per 256-fragment stride), barycentric in-triangle test, single byte write `dev_image[(pyPixel)*width + pxPixel] = 255` to LINEAR uint8 memory. The DRR-family techniques were designed for volumetric ray casts/splats; their transfer value is mostly negative or deferred:

| Technique (source) | What it is | Verdict for JTML | Cost in this stack |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bindless texture objects (abdellah L70–74, L283–287) | Runtime-created texture objects over cudaArrays (3D-locality layout, trilinear filter); needs Kepler 3.0+/CUDA 5.0+ | DEFER — accelerates READ-side locality on volumetric data; JTML's fill is a scatter-WRITE to linear memory (no texture benefit); only the metric kernels read dev_image_ (edge/dilate/chamfer neighborhoods) and those crops are small, already L2-served. Only adopt if Cut 0's ncu shows the metric kernels cache-bound (L1/L2 miss-rate evidence) | 3 kernels touched + texture-object lifecycle per buffer; medium code, LOW-MEDIUM regression risk (changed cache behavior is a perf gamble, not a semantics risk; tex1Dfetch is value-exact) |
| CUDA/OpenGL interop (abdellah L276–280) | PBO mapping of the CUDA image into an OpenGL texture for DISPLAY; buffers locked while mapped | NO-GO for the cost path — display-only in the paper; JTML's display is VTK/cvMat D2H (render_engine.cu:852–856, :880–884), OFF the hot path. Any zero-copy display is angle 04's VTK-surface domain, not a perf cut | Would touch the visualization path, not compute; skip |
| Block projection / slab reuse (Mu 2016: muFastDRRGeneration2016.txt L135–140, L147–148, L232–234) | Pose-grid of pre-generated block projections; new poses re-assemble slabs ("reuses ray segments instead of whole rays"); bounded, estimable projection error (<0.5 mm at ≤3° off-grid, Eq. 2) | NO-GO — an approximate-reuse scheme for EXPENSIVE volumetric ray casts. JTML's re-projection is already the cheapest part of the eval; the pose-grid/slab machinery costs more than the re-render AND breaks the bit-identity/determinism contract every cut is gated on (R1 determinism finding: int-atomics + bit-identical diffing). The error-bound idea has a legitimate home in the ablation's resolution axis (R3-8), never in the cost path | Full new subsystem (pose grid, slab storage, error bookkeeping) + accuracy loss; excluded |
| Splatting (wobbled splatting — Spörk via dorgham refs [22],[30],[31]; zwickerSurfaceSplatting2001 in corpus) | Object-space forward projection of voxels/samples as screen-space footprints | NO-GO — replaces the barycentric-exact fill with approximate footprints (overlap/underlap, fuzzy edges); changes the rendered image, breaks bit-identity. The fill's barycentric test IS the exactness; the dilation metric absorbs small edge fuzz but the determinism contract does not | New fill kernel + per-vertex splat data; high risk; excluded |
| Sampled / reduced-resolution DRR (tornai RR1/RR2 L21–23; dorgham RR1/RR2 §III-B) | Render a subset of rays/pixels/samples, interpolate; registration-accuracy-preserving at 50% compression, NOT at 75% (dorgham Fig. 13) | ARM-ABLE — the one family technique with a real home, as a VALUE-CHANGING ablation axis (render-resolution scaling, see R3-8), never as a bit-identical cut | Low (scale memset/fill dims + metrics at scale or upscale); gated by oracle + z-profile probe |
| Block-size / occupancy tuning (tornai §III: 10–145% execution-time swings with block size; optimal blocks/SM 1–8, vendor-suggested sizes often NOT optimal; abdellah §IV: block-config profiling with cudaEventRecord) | Launch-config-only tuning; kernel semantics unchanged | FREE WIN CANDIDATE — JTML's threads_per_block=256 is a single constant (include/compute/cuda_launch_parameters.h); a sweep {64,128,256,512} on FillTriangleKernel/StridePrefixKernel + the metric kernels is zero-semantics (identical kernel behavior, different launch config) and belongs in Cut 0's ncu pass. Matters MORE if Cut 3's fixed grid lands (large empty-grid block counts, R2-3) | One constant + re-measure; zero risk; the paper's own cudaEventRecord methodology matches Cut 0's |
| Auto-differentiable DRR (gopalakrishnan 2022) | Vectorized Siddon in PyTorch with autograd | NOT a render-acceleration technique — a differentiability technique. Perf-relevant for three things: (a) the torch-route is ~50–100× slower per pixel than hand CUDA (72.7 ms/200² = ~1.8 µs/px on a 2080 Ti vs tornai's ~30 ns/px on a 580 GTX) → corroborates the torch-boundary NO-GO for the eval path (04 contradiction 5; 06 photometric NO-GO); (b) registration-level evidence for angle 06: 745/1000 converged in 65.5±14.3 iterations (1.92±0.43 s) with negative ZNCC "locally convex in the neighborhood of the optimal" (L32–34, L360–361, L618, L639–641) — the field's gradient-based registration uses ~2 orders fewer iterations than DIRECT's thousands, so IF the polish arm lands, per-eval speed matters more, strengthening the cuts; (c) gradient-vs-FFD fidelity 0.05±0.01 (L314–316) — the field standard that angle 06's gradient-twin gate mirrors | None for the eval path; the numbers feed 06's premises |
| Matched forward/back projectors (kim 2023, kimDifferentiableForwardProjector2023.txt L212–221) | "one should employ methods for backprojection that are the exact transpose of the forward projection, referred to as matched projectors"; chosen "because... stable after over a thousand or more iterations"; torch-free C++/CUDA core + thin torch.nn.Module binding, small memory footprint | CORROBORATION ONLY — the architecture pattern (CUDA core + thin adapter, no per-call allocation) is already JTML's compute/manager split; the matched-projector doctrine is already folded into 04 R3-4 / 06 R2-4; the "thousand+ iterations" stability note supports keeping JTML's forward path exact (no approximate reuse) in a 35k-eval regime | None (already carried by 04/06) |

- Severity: medium-high (the verdicts bound the "beyond Cut 3" space: nothing in the fast-DRR family rescues the fragment-fill itself; the wins are the resolution axis, the block-size knob, and the launch-overhead contingency of R3-3).
- Confidence: medium (analytical verdicts grounded in paper definitions + verified kernel structure; not measured).
- Relevance: Cut 3's mechanics (rounds 1–2: device-side clamp + fixed grid, bit-safe via in-kernel guards) stand as specified — the family adds no better fragment-fill mechanism; its license is for the areas AROUND the fill.

#### R3-5 — Dorgham's "similarity on the GPU" doctrine = the primary-text antecedent of Cuts 1–3

#### R3-5 — Dorgham's "similarity on the GPU" doctrine = the primary-text antecedent of Cuts 1–3

Whereas transforming the DRRs from the device memory to the host memory requires almost the same time" (the D2H copy is a first-class cost — the "synchronization problem" framing is at L570-578: GPU-side similarity "does not require any data transfer between the device and the host memory... there will not be a delay or synchronization problem but more device memory will be required to store the DRR").

A scheme that simultaneously renders the silhouette for each of these hyper-rectangles would scale almost proportionally up to this number." — the DIRECT+silhouette field's own identified scaling path is EXACTLY Cut 2 (iteration batching: collect the iteration's potentially-optimal boxes, enqueue all evals back-to-back on double-buffered state, one terminal wait, replay bookkeeping). Flood's "at the very least two, and in practice can be much higher" matches JTML's 2×N_optimal evals per TrisectPotentiallyOptimal iteration (direct_optimizer.cpp:113–163).
- Also noted: Flood's own "potentially optimal" phrasing confirms the DIRECT hull-selection structure the batch surface must preserve (the A/B ordering + replay contract of R2/Cut 2).
- Confidence: high (verbatim). Relevance: Cut 2 goes from "a JTML-invented optimization" to "the lineage's documented scaling path, implemented 8 years later".

#### R3-8 — Beyond the cuts: the render-resolution ablation arm (the one family technique with a real home)

- Field evidence for the arm: Dorgham's registration accuracy is "almost the same" as full-resolution at 50% sampling compression and "did not provide an accurate result" at 75% (dorghamGPUAcceleratedGeneration2012.txt, Fig. 12–13, §IV-B); Tornai shows 1.1–9.1% sampled DRRs used successfully in registration with robustness (L21–23, L550–552: 200–700 DRRs per registration); the trunk stage of the lineage runs at dilation 6–10 (blurred), which is exactly the regime where resolution loss is cheapest.
